Market attractiveness is moderate on paper but unproven in practice, and the plan does little to substantiate it. The problem is real: surplus and cosmetically imperfect produce is well documented, and restaurant margin pressure is genuine. But the plan's market sizing is entirely top-down and rhetorical ('thousands of farms, tens of thousands of restaurants, multi-billion dollar waste problem, a small percent is a big business'). It offers no TAM/SAM/SOM, no estimate of seconds volume or dollar value, no average transaction size, and no analysis of how much of the wasted-food figure is actually monetizable. Food waste value is not the same as addressable transaction value: seconds are sold at deep discounts, so a 10-15% commission on low-priced, low-volume, irregular lots may yield very thin revenue per transaction. A bottom-up model (number of small farms within delivery range of a metro x seconds pounds per week x realistic price x take rate, plus restaurant/cannery purchasing volume) is needed to test whether a single region is even viable, let alone a national business.

Targeting: the target groups are directionally right but each has weaknesses. Small farms near cities are a reasonable supply side, but the plan itself notes they are time-poor; seconds supply is also seasonal, perishable, and unpredictable, which hurts listing reliability. Restaurants are the weaker demand side: independent restaurants buy in small quantities, have thin staff, and value consistency and delivery convenience over a slightly lower price, so they may not tolerate variable lots and DIY pickup. Canneries and preservers are likely the better demand anchor because they buy bulk and care less about uniformity, yet they are mentioned only in passing and are not segmented or validated. The plan should identify which demand segment actually anchors volume (cannery/processors, institutional kitchens, commissaries, juice/sauce makers) and quantify it. Logistics and cold-chain/pickup friction is the central unaddressed barrier on both sides.

Competitive dynamics and defensibility weaken attractiveness. The plan admits the space is crowded (surplus-food apps, gleaning/food-rescue nonprofits, wholesale distributors and brokers, farm-to-restaurant platforms such as those already serving local sourcing). The claimed differentiation (seconds-only, small farms, B2B, analytics) is a positioning choice, not a barrier. The data/analytics 'moat' is speculative: it requires substantial transaction volume that a localized seconds marketplace may never reach, and network effects are asserted rather than demonstrated, especially since the market is hyper-local and each region must be rebuilt from scratch, which limits true network effects and makes customer acquisition costs unlikely to fall as claimed. Disintermediation is also a risk: once a farm and a chef or cannery connect, they can transact off-platform and avoid the commission.

Scalability and exit potential: the market could plausibly support a regional, capital-light business, but the venture-scale case is not made. Region-by-region expansion with local onboarding and logistics staffing is operationally heavy, and low-value perishable transactions with a modest take rate imply weak unit economics and slow path to scale. Revenue streams beyond commission (subscriptions, data sales) are untested, and no willingness-to-pay evidence exists. The 'three years to profitability' claim is unsupported. Likely exit paths are therefore limited: acquisition by a larger food-service distributor, produce marketplace, food-waste platform, or sustainability-focused agtech/foodtech company seeking supply-side access in small-farm networks, or a mission-aligned/lifestyle business or nonprofit-adjacent hybrid. A large strategic exit or IPO is unlikely unless the company proves strong repeat transaction volume, retained supply and demand, and a defensible logistics or data advantage. Acquirers would value demonstrated GMV, retention, and farmer/buyer density in specific geographies, none of which exist yet.

Bottom line: a real problem and a sensible beachhead, but the market opportunity is asserted rather than demonstrated. To raise attractiveness, the team should build a bottom-up market model, identify and validate the anchor demand segment (likely processors/canneries), test willingness to pay and take rate, quantify repeat usage from the early pilot users, and address logistics and disintermediation. Until then, the venture looks like a viable regional or niche business with a modest, strategic-acquisition-style exit rather than a clearly scalable, high-return venture.

Business plan text:

Gleanwell
Executive Summary
Gleanwell: Connecting Small Farms and Restaurants With Seconds Produce
Problem
Food waste is a huge problem in the United States and around the world. Alot of this waste
happens at the farm level. Small farms grow produce and some of it comes out as what is called
seconds, meaning it is not perfect looking, it is to ripe, it is to small or to big, or it has
a blemish. Grocery stores and farmers markets dont want seconds so the farmers has nowhere to
sell them. Many small farms is also very busy and does not have time to call around to
restaurants or canneries to find a buyer. So the seconds produce goes to waste or gets
composted or left in the field. This is a loss of money for the farmer and a loss of food for
the world. At the same time, restaurants have rising ingredient costs and chefs are always
looking for lower cost ingredients especially for soups, sauces, stocks and specials where the
looks of the produce does not matter. Canneries and preservers also need large amounts of
produce at low price. So there is a problem on both sides that nobody is connecting. The farmer
has produce and no buyer, the chef needs produce and has no cheap source.
Solution
Gleanwell is a app that solve this problem by connecting small farms with seconds produce to
nearby restaurants and canneries. The farmer opens the app and posts a listing of what they
have, for example forty pounds of tomatoes that are very ripe, with a price and a pickup
window. Chefs and cannery buyers near the farm get notified and can browse listings, claim what
they want, and arrange pickup or delivery. Our platform is a win win for everyone. Farms earn
money from produce that would of been wasted, chefs get lower cost ingredients, and the
environment benefits from less waste. We also are building a data and analytics layer that will
use the listing data to help farmers predict how much surplus they will have and to price there
seconds better over time. We beleive this data will become a very valuable asset for the whole
food supply chain and gives Gleanwell a strong moat.
Market
The market for our product is very large. There are thousands of small farms in the United
States and tens of thousands of restaurants and many canneries. Food waste is a multi billion
dollar problem. If we only capture a small percent of this market it would be a very big
business. Our target customers are first small farms within a short drive of a city and second
restaurants and canneries in that same area. We will start local in one region and then expand
region by region as we grow. We think the farm to restaurant trend and the growing interest in
sustainability and local food is a big tailwind for us. Consumers care more and more about
waste and chefs like to say they source local, so our app fits perfect into this trend.
Business Model
Our business model is a marketplace model. We plan to take a commission on each transaction
that happens on the platform, probably something like ten to fifteen percent, but we are still
figuring out the right number. We may also later charge a subscription fee for the premium
analytics features for farms and for restaurants who want priority access to listings. Another
possible revenue stream is selling the data and insights to other companies in the food
industry. We have not yet tested what price farmers and chefs are willing to pay so these
numbers is an estimate and will be validated as we get more users. Our costs include building
and maintaining the app, hosting, marketing to farms and restaurants, and someone to manage
logistics and onboarding. We believe that as the network grows the cost to acquire each new
user will go down because of network effects.
Competition

The space of food waste and food marketplaces is crowded and there is many players. There are
other apps that sell surplus food to consumers, there are food rescue nonprofits and food banks
that take donations from farms, there are wholesale produce distributors and brokers, and there
are farm to restaurant ordering platforms. Some of these overlap with what we do. However we
think Gleanwell is different because we focus only on seconds produce from small farms and we
connect directly to restaurants and canneries, not to consumers, and because of our data and
analytics layer. Other competitors dont focus on small farms who is underserved. Our advantage
is that we is a nimble startup that is close to the local community and understand both sides
of the market. We know that larger players could enter our space but we think we can move
faster and build relationships first.
Team
Our team is three students at our university. Dalton Verhaegen is the CEO and leads business
development and strategy and is studying business and has worked at a restaurant and so
understands chef needs. Priyanka Oyelaran-Webb is the CTO and leads the app development and
data and she is studying computer science and has built several apps for class projects. Marcus
Teodorescu is responsible for operations and farm relationships and grew up around a family
farm and so knows the problems of small farms firsthand. Together we have the passion, the
skills and the vision to make Gleanwell succeed. We are very commited to this idea and willing
to work hard.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have reached two important milestones. First we have defined our core business
concept, including who our customers are and how the app would work. Second we have got our
first external users on the product, which are a small number of farms and a few restaurants
who have tried the app. We also have a website. We have not formed our legal entity yet but
plan to do so soon, probably as an LLC or maybe a C corp, we are still deciding. We have not
generated any significant revenue yet and so far the work has been paid by ourselves with our
own time. For the next year we expect costs for development, hosting, marketing, and a part
time hire for logistics. We project that in year one we will have a small number of
transactions, then grow quickly in year two and three as we expand to more regions and add the
analytics subscription. We think we could reach profitability in about three years but this
depend on how fast we grow the network. Our financial projections is still early and we plan to
refine them with the feedback from the competition and mentors.
What We Ask For
We are applying to this business plan competition for several reasons. First we hope to win
prize funding which we would use to form our legal entity, improve the app, and run a bigger
pilot with more farms and restaurants in our region. Second we would like mentorship from
experienced entrepreneurs and judges who can help us with our business model, pricing, and how
to scale. Third we want connections to potential investors, farm and restaurant partners, and
other resources in the food industry. We belive that with the right support Gleanwell can grow
into a major player in the food and beverage space and make a real impact on food waste while
helping farms and chefs. Thank you for considering our application and we look forward to the
opportunity to pitch to you.

Question: Share thoughts on market attractiveness and exit potential. Address whether the market would support this venture, whether the company targets the correct group, and whether the market is large enough to support scaling.
